the-ruin.control: Principality of Moldavia under Ottoman control; Polish incursions
the-ruin.summary: Ottoman forces used Khotyn as a base for the 1672 conquest of Podolia. In 1673 Jan Sobieski destroyed an Ottoman army at Khotyn, and Polish garrisons held parts of the area in the following years.

hetmanate-decline.control: Moldavia (Bukovina) and Ottoman Empire (Khotyn raya from 1713)
hetmanate-decline.summary: The Ottomans placed Khotyn under direct rule as a raya in 1713 and modernized the fortress. Russian armies won at Stavuchany in 1739 and took Khotyn, but returned it under the Treaty of Belgrade.
hetmanate-decline.military: Battle of Stavuchany (1739); Russian capture of Khotyn in 1739 and 1769.

partitions-crimea.summary: In 1775 Austria annexed the northwestern corner of Moldavia as Bukovina, with Czernowitz as its center. Khotyn remained Ottoman and was besieged by Austrian and Russian forces in 1788.
partitions-crimea.military: Siege of Khotyn (1788) during the Austro-Russian-Turkish war.

two-empires.control: Austrian Empire (Bukovina) and Russian Empire (Khotyn, from 1812)
two-empires.summary: Bukovina was attached to Galicia in 1786 and became a separate crown land, the Duchy of Bukovina, in 1849; German, Jewish, Romanian, Ukrainian and Polish communities shaped Czernowitz. The Treaty of Bucharest (1812) gave Khotyn to Russia within Bessarabia.
two-empires.military: Lukian Kobylytsia led a Hutsul peasant revolt in 1843-1848.

national-revival.summary: Czernowitz University opened in 1875, and Ukrainian writers Yurii Fedkovych and Olha Kobylianska worked there; the city hosted the 1908 Yiddish language conference. The Residence of Bukovinian Metropolitans was completed in 1882.
national-revival.military: Russian troops occupied Czernowitz several times in 1914-1917; the Brusilov Offensive took it in June 1916.
places: Residence of Bukovinian and Dalmatian Metropolitans

ukrainian-revolution.control: Briefly Ukrainian (ZUNR), then Kingdom of Romania (from November 1918)
ukrainian-revolution.summary: A Ukrainian assembly in Chernivtsi on 3 November 1918 claimed northern Bukovina for the West Ukrainian state, but Romanian troops occupied the city on 11 November and a General Congress voted for union with Romania on 28 November. Bessarabia, including Khotyn, joined Romania in 1918.
ukrainian-revolution.military: Romanian army occupation of Bukovina in November 1918.

soviet-takeover.summary: Peasants in the Khotyn area rose against Romanian rule in January 1919 and were bloodily suppressed. The Treaty of Saint-Germain (1919) confirmed Bukovina for Romania, and the 1920 Treaty of Paris recognized its Bessarabian rule.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: Romanian authorities closed Ukrainian schools, Romanianized Chernivtsi University and administration, and imposed a state of siege in Bessarabian districts.

holodomor-terror.summary: The Dniester border separated the area from the Holodomor in the Soviet Moldavian ASSR and Ukraine. Romanian royal dictatorship from 1938 further restricted minorities; Ukrainian nationalist youth groups operated underground.

soviet-annexations.summary: After a Soviet ultimatum, the Red Army occupied northern Bukovina, the Hertsa region and Khotyn in June 1940, and Chernivtsi Oblast was formed. Deportations followed, and in April 1941 Soviet border guards shot Romanian villagers trying to cross to Romania at Fântâna Albă.

links.title: Soviet occupation of Bessarabia and Northern Bukovina

nazi-occupation.control: Kingdom of Romania (Axis ally) until spring 1944; then USSR
nazi-occupation.summary: Romanian and German troops retook the area in July 1941; Jews were murdered or confined in the Czernowitz ghetto and deported to Transnistria, though mayor Traian Popovici saved about 20,000. The Red Army returned in March-April 1944.
nazi-occupation.military: The Proskurov-Chernovtsy Offensive retook the region in spring 1944.

postwar-ussr.summary: The 1947 Paris Peace Treaty confirmed the Soviet border. Many Romanians, Germans and Jews left or were deported, and collectivization and repression targeted both Romanian and Ukrainian villages.
postwar-ussr.military: OUN-UPA groups operated in the Bukovinian Carpathians until the early 1950s.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: Chernivtsi University occupied the former Metropolitans' Residence, and the city produced pop stars Sofia Rotaru and Volodymyr Ivasiuk, whose mysterious death in 1979 sparked protests. A 1988 outbreak of child hair loss blamed on chemical pollution caused alarm.

independence.summary: The 1997 Ukrainian-Romanian treaty settled the border; the oblast's Romanian minority, concentrated around Hertsa and Hlyboka, gained cultural rights, and cross-border trade grew.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The Residence of Bukovinian and Dalmatian Metropolitans was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2011. The oblast supported the Orange Revolution and Euromaidan.
places: Residence of Bukovinian and Dalmatian Metropolitans

links.title: Residence of Bukovinian and Dalmatian Metropolitans

crimea-donbas-war.summary: Men from the oblast were mobilized and volunteered for the Donbas war, while Chernivtsi hosted displaced families.

full-scale-invasion.summary: Chernivtsi received large numbers of displaced people, and crossings to Romania at Porubne and Moldova at Mamalyha became major refugee routes. The oblast was rarely struck in 2022.

war-of-attrition.summary: The oblast remained one of the safest in Ukraine, though occasional drones and missiles reached it during attacks on western Ukraine; Russian drones repeatedly strayed into neighboring Romanian and Moldovan airspace.

war-2025-2026.summary: Massed raids on western Ukraine hit Chernivtsi more often in 2025, including a June 2025 attack that reportedly killed at least two people in the city. Information on 2026 is limited.

UA-68.name: Khmelnytskyi Oblast
UA-68.overview: Khmelnytskyi Oblast joins western Podolia, with the Dniester canyon and the fortress city of Kamianets-Podilskyi, to southern Volhynia around Iziaslav, Polonne and Starokostiantyniv. Trypillian and Scythian-era farmers were followed by Slavic tribes and, in Rus' times, by the Bolokhovian land and Bakota, the Mongol-era center of Podolia. From the 1360s the Lithuanian Koriatovych princes and then Poland ruled Podolia from Kamianets, which the Ottomans held as a provincial capital in 1672-1699; Khmelnytsky's Cossacks fought major battles here at Pyliavtsi and Zhvanets. Russian from 1793, the area was briefly the last stronghold of the Ukrainian People's Republic in 1919, then a Soviet border region on the Zbruch, scene of the 1941 Kamianets-Podilskyi massacre. Today it hosts the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant and the Starokostiantyniv air base, a frequent Russian target.

trypillia.summary: Trypillian villages lined the Dniester terraces and the upper Southern Bug; sites in the Kamianets area belong to the western Trypillian groups with richly painted pottery.

bronze-age-steppe.control: Corded Ware, Komarów and Bilohrudivka cultures
bronze-age-steppe.summary: After the Trypillian decline Corded Ware herders and later Komarów (Trzciniec circle) communities spread over the Podolian upland, with steppe Yamnaya barrows reaching the southeast.

cimmerians.summary: The Dniester valley belonged to Thracian Hallstatt groups, while eastern districts lay near the Chornolis culture of the forest-steppe, which built hillforts against Cimmerian raids.
cimmerians.military: Early hillforts were raised against steppe raiders.

scythians.control: Podolian forest-steppe farmers under Scythian cultural influence
scythians.summary: The Podolian group of the Scythian-era forest-steppe culture, possibly the 'agricultural Scythians' or Alazones of Herodotus, built hillforts and barrows and traded with Greek Tyras and Olbia.
scythians.military: Scythian-period hillforts protected settlements on the Southern Bug and Dniester tributaries.

sarmatians.control: Lipița, Przeworsk and Zarubintsy-related groups; Sarmatians to the southeast
sarmatians.summary: Dacian-related Lipița groups lived on the Dniester and Przeworsk and Zarubintsy-related communities further north, while Sarmatians held the steppe.

goths-chernyakhov.control: Chernyakhov culture (Goths, Sarmatians, Slavs and others)
goths-chernyakhov.summary: The area was densely settled by the Chernyakhov culture, with villages, pottery workshops and Roman coin hoards on the Dniester and Southern Bug.

huns.summary: The Chernyakhov villages collapsed after the Hunnic invasion of 375, and population declined.

antes.control: Sclaveni (Prague-Korchak) in the north; Antes (Penkovka) in the south
antes.summary: The area lay at the junction of the Prague-Korchak culture of the Sclaveni and the Penkovka culture associated with the Antes.

east-slavic-tribes.summary: The Volhynian north was held by the Dulebe-Buzhan tribes, and the Dniester south by the Tivertsi; hillfort settlements stood on the Smotrych and Sluch.

kyivan-rus-formation.control: East Slavic tribes, made tributary to Kyiv
kyivan-rus-formation.summary: The Tivertsi and their neighbors were drawn into the Kyivan sphere, taking part in campaigns against Byzantium, while Pechenegs threatened from the south.

kyivan-rus-volodymyr.summary: Volodymyr's rule extended over the area, linking it to Volhynia in the north and the Dniester trade route in the south.

kyivan-rus-peak.summary: The area lay between Volhynia and the Dniester frontier; settlements grew along the Horyn and Sluch in the north.

rus-fragmentation.control: Principalities of Galicia and Volhynia; the semi-independent Bolokhovian land
rus-fragmentation.summary: The Dniester south belonged to Galicia, with the rock-cut Bakota monastery above the river, and the north to Volhynia. Between them lay the Bolokhovian land, whose towns kept a degree of autonomy.

galicia-volhynia.summary: Roman Mstyslavych and Daniel ruled the area, but the Bolokhovian princes allied with Daniel's rivals and later with the Mongols.
galicia-volhynia.military: Daniel fought the Bolokhovian princes in the 1230s.

mongol-period.control: Golden Horde (Podolia under Tatar baskaks); Galicia-Volhynia in the north
mongol-period.summary: Podolia passed under direct Mongol overlordship; Bakota was the seat of a Tatar baskak in the 1250s. Daniel destroyed the Bolokhovian towns for collaborating with the Horde.
mongol-period.military: Daniel's 1255 campaign against the Bolokhovian and Tatar-allied towns.

lithuania-poland.control: Lithuanian Koriatovych princes, then Poland (Podolian Voivodeship); Lithuanian Volhynia in the north
lithuania-poland.summary: After Algirdas's victory at Blue Waters (1362) the Koriatovych princes made Kamianets the capital of Podolia, granting it Magdeburg rights in 1374. Western Podolia passed to Poland in 1430s as the Podolian Voivodeship, and Kostiantyn Ostrozky founded Starokostiantyniv in 1561.
lithuania-poland.military: Kamianets-Podilskyi Castle and Medzhybizh Castle defended against Tatar raids.

commonwealth.summary: Kamianets-Podilskyi was the Commonwealth's main bulwark against the Ottomans, a city of Polish, Ruthenian and Armenian quarters. Magnates fortified Medzhybizh, Starokostiantyniv and Polonne.
commonwealth.military: Kamianets was considered an impregnable fortress; Tatar raids were frequent.

cossack-hetmanate.control: Contested between the Commonwealth and the Cossack Hetmanate (Podilia regiment)
cossack-hetmanate.summary: Khmelnytsky routed the Polish army at Pyliavtsi in September 1648, and Maksym Kryvonis stormed Polonne. The area changed hands repeatedly, and the 1653 siege of Zhvanets ended in a truce.
cossack-hetmanate.military: Battle of Pyliavtsi (1648), Siege of Polonne (1648), Siege of Zhvanets (1653).

the-ruin.control: Ottoman Empire (Podolia Eyalet, capital Kamianets) 1672-1699; Poland in the north
the-ruin.summary: Sultan Mehmed IV took Kamianets in 1672 and made it the capital of the Ottoman province of Podolia; the cathedral was turned into a mosque with a minaret that still stands. Hetman Petro Doroshenko allied with the Ottomans.

hetmanate-decline.summary: Poland regained Podolia in 1699. The Baal Shem Tov, founder of Hasidism, lived and taught in Medzhybizh from about 1740, and a disputation with the Frankists took place in Kamianets in 1757.

partitions-crimea.summary: The Second Partition (1793) gave the area to Russia; Kamianets-Podilskyi became the seat of the Podolia Governorate, while the Volhynian north joined the Volhynian Governorate.

two-empires.summary: Ustym Karmaliuk led a long peasant rebellion against landlords across Podolia from 1813 until his death in 1835. Polish nobles kept the estates, and Jewish shtetls such as Medzhybizh flourished.
two-empires.military: Polish insurgents fought in Podolia in 1831; Kamianets fortress lost its military role.

national-revival.summary: Railways bypassed Kamianets but made Proskuriv (today's Khmelnytskyi) a growing junction town. Ukrainian cultural societies formed under tsarist restrictions, and in World War I the area was a staging ground for the Southwestern Front.
national-revival.military: Austro-Hungarian troops briefly entered the Zbruch borderland in 1914.

ukrainian-revolution.summary: The area belonged to the UNR and Skoropadsky's Hetmanate; the Kamianets-Podilskyi Ukrainian State University opened in October 1918 under Ivan Ohienko.

soviet-takeover.control: UNR (temporary capital Kamianets-Podilskyi, 1919), Polish occupation, then Soviet Ukraine
soviet-takeover.summary: In February 1919 UNR troops carried out the Proskurov pogrom, killing over 1,000 Jews. From June to November 1919 Kamianets-Podilskyi was the UNR's temporary capital, then came under Polish control; the Bolsheviks took the area in November 1920.
soviet-takeover.military: The UNR army made its last stand here before crossing the Zbruch into Polish internment in November 1920.

soviet-ukraine-1920s.summary: The Zbruch became the Soviet-Polish border, and the area was a militarized frontier zone. Collectivization from 1929 provoked peasant revolts in Podolian villages in 1930.
soviet-ukraine-1920s.military: Soviet border troops guarded the Zbruch frontier.

holodomor-terror.summary: The Holodomor killed many villagers in Podolia. In 1935-1936 thousands of Poles and Germans were deported from the border zone to Kazakhstan, and Kamianets-Podilskyi Oblast was created in 1937.
holodomor-terror.military: Fortified regions of the Stalin Line were built near Letychiv and Kamianets-Podilskyi.

soviet-annexations.summary: The oblast served as a staging area for the Soviet invasion of Poland in September 1939, after which it was no longer a border region; the oblast seat moved to Proskuriv in 1941.
soviet-annexations.military: Soviet armies crossed the Zbruch from here on 17 September 1939.

nazi-occupation.control: Nazi Germany (Reichskommissariat Ukraine; briefly Hungarian military administration)
nazi-occupation.summary: In late August 1941 German units murdered about 23,600 Jews at Kamianets-Podilskyi, including thousands deported from Hungary. The Red Army retook the area in March-April 1944, when German forces were encircled in the Kamianets-Podilskyi pocket.
nazi-occupation.military: Kamenets-Podolsky pocket (Hube's Pocket) during the Proskurov-Chernovtsy offensive.

postwar-ussr.summary: The area suffered in the 1946-1947 famine. In 1954, for the 300th anniversary of the Pereiaslav agreement, Proskuriv was renamed Khmelnytskyi and the oblast took the same name.
postwar-ussr.military: UPA groups were active in the oblast's Volhynian north until about 1950.

soviet-ukraine-late.summary: Khmelnytskyi became an industrial city, Kamianets-Podilskyi a historical reserve, and the Khmelnytskyi Nuclear Power Plant at Netishyn began operating in 1987.
soviet-ukraine-late.military: Starokostiantyniv hosted a major Soviet air base.

independence.summary: Khmelnytskyi's huge wholesale market became one of the largest in Eastern Europe, while Kamianets-Podilskyi developed tourism around its castle.
independence.military: The 7th Tactical Aviation Brigade with Su-24 bombers was based at Starokostiantyniv.

orange-to-euromaidan.summary: The oblast backed Yushchenko in 2004; on 19 February 2014 a shooting at the SBU building in Khmelnytskyi killed a protester during Euromaidan.

crimea-donbas-war.summary: Units and volunteers from the oblast served in the Donbas, and the Khmelnytskyi-based 8th Special Purpose Regiment fought there.
crimea-donbas-war.military: The 8th Special Purpose Regiment took part in the battles of 2014-2015.

full-scale-invasion.summary: Starokostiantyniv air base was hit on the first day of the invasion and repeatedly thereafter; the oblast received many displaced people.
full-scale-invasion.military: Su-24 bombers from Starokostiantyniv later launched Storm Shadow cruise missiles.

war-of-attrition.summary: Missile and drone attacks targeted Starokostiantyniv and Khmelnytskyi; a November 2023 drone strike in nearby Slavuta damaged buildings and cut power lines at the Khmelnytskyi NPP, according to the IAEA.
war-of-attrition.military: Starokostiantyniv air base remained one of Russia's most frequently attacked targets.

war-2025-2026.summary: Strikes on the Starokostiantyniv air base and on energy infrastructure continued, and explosions were reported in Khmelnytskyi during the November 2025 attack on western Ukraine. Information on 2026 is limited.
war-2025-2026.military: Starokostiantyniv remained a key Ukrainian air base and target.
